newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines braces for drought brought by El Nino.
newsitem.headline: Philippines braces for drought brought by El Nino.

text.p: Philippine agriculture and weather experts on Friday said a drought brought on by the El Nino effect could be the worst in years, but measures were underway to mitigate the impact on crops.

"Based on changes in the (Pacific's) sea surface temperature, this year's El Nino would be comparable in intensity with what happened in 1982-83," Nathaniel Cruz, meteorologist at the Philippine weather bureau, said at an El Nino forum.

Cruz said the Philippine Atmospheric Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa) had detected signs of changes in wind patterns and higher temperatures in the Pacific as early as April.

The country has suffered severe drops in crop harvests, particularly rice, in at least five droughts brought by El Nino episodes in the past 16 years, said Rolando Dy, executive director of the Center for food and Agribusiness at the University of Asia and the Pacific.

El Nino is caused by the warming of water in the western Pacific Ocean, which interacts with other weather systems and typically produces freak weather such as drought in some areas and heavier-than-normal rainfall in others.
The 1983 El Nino caused withering drought in Australia, Indonesia, the Philippines and South Africa, while floods inundated India and Peru and severe winter storms lashed California.
In 1983, Philippine crop harvests dropped by 7.4 percent, he said.
The 1982-83 drought destroyed 590,000 tonnes of unmilled rice and devastated 170,000 tonnes of corn.

"The 1997-98 drought is a foregone conclusion. Experts project that it will be as severe as the 1982-1983 drought," Dy said as he urged the government to import about 950,000 tonnes of rice for delivery in the first half of 1998.
Dy said he expected Philippine rice harvests to drop by 15 percent to 2.7 million tonnes in the first half of 1998 from 3.2 million in the first half of 1997.
Government agriculture experts said the country has enough food supplies, particularly rice, for the rest of 1997.
"I'm not pessimistic on crop losses in 1997, but 1998 would be a difficult year," said Bureau of Soils and Water Management director Rogelio Concepcion.
"We listen to the bad signals," he said, adding that his agency had begun cloud seeding in areas experiencing low rainfall in recent weeks. "We will be above the dams by October," he said.
Rice planted between October and November will be harvested early next year.
The effects of the lower rainfall would be felt starting in the last quarter of 1997, said Pagasa director Leoncio Amadore.
"Weather monitoring from April to June showed below normal precipitation," he said.

Besides cloud seeding, Agriculture Secretary Salvador Escudero said the government has dug 1,448 wells to irrigate 7,240 hectares of farmland nationwide and has constructed water reservoirs and new irrigation facilities.

The Agriculture department has started a campaign among farmers to plant short maturing rice and corn varieties to minimise their vulnerability to potential damage from either extended drought or floods and typhoons.
